Getting started with tulpaObs

Source: vignettes/quickstart.Rmd
quickstart.Rmd

Installation 

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/tulpaObs")            # latest from GitHub
pak::pak("gcol33/tulpaObs@v0.1.1")     # a specific tagged release

Tagged releases are listed at https://github.com/gcol33/tulpaObs/releases.

pak resolves the dependency tree, pulling tulpa and tulpaMesh from the r-universe repository DESCRIPTION declares in Additional_repositories, at or above the Imports floor. A C++17 toolchain is needed (Rtools on Windows, Xcode CLI tools on macOS, r-base-dev on Linux); both tulpa and tulpaObs compile their backends on first install.

library(tulpaObs)

What tulpaObs fits

A survey that visits a site a handful of times and records whether a species was seen carries two things at once: whether the species is there at all, and whether you happened to detect it on a given visit. tulpaObs fits the hierarchical models that separate those two. You pass the latent process formula, a detection formula, the detection-history matrix y, and a family; tobs() builds the design, plugs the family likelihood into the tulpa engine, and returns a fitted object you can summarise, predict from, and compare.

The package covers occupancy (single-season, dynamic, community, integrated, joint species distribution), N-mixture abundance (single species and community, Poisson or negative binomial), and a vegetation cover hurdle. Spatial fields, temporal structure, and random effects attach to any of them through terms inside the formula. The default engine is a fast Laplace approximation; the same model fits under NUTS when you want the full posterior.

The split that defines the package is between the state and the observation. The state is the thing you care about: occupied or not, how many individuals, what fraction of ground a plant covers. The observation is what the field crew wrote down, and it is the state seen through a detection process that misses some of what is there. A naive analysis reads the observation as the state and undercounts everywhere detection is below one. Every family in tulpaObs writes the two levels separately, integrates the latent state out of the likelihood in closed form where it can, and reports both the state coefficients and the detection coefficients. You read occupancy against a background that already accounts for the visits where the species was present and missed.

Where this differs from the tools next to it is the engine underneath. tulpaObs is a thin observation layer; the inference lives in tulpa, which composes a fast deterministic approximation with an exact sampler. The Laplace path finds the posterior mode and the curvature there and returns in a fraction of a second, which is the right tool for the first look and for comparing candidate models. The NUTS path samples the full posterior and reports Rhat and effective sample size, which is the right tool when detection is low, visits are few, or the posterior is skewed enough that a Gaussian summary at the mode would mislead. The same tobs() call switches between them with one argument, and the fitted object answers the same accessors either way. Against unmarked, the draw is a Bayesian posterior with credible intervals rather than a maximum-likelihood point fit; against a hand-written Stan model, the draw is the speed of the deterministic path and a formula interface that reads like lme4. You write the model once and choose the inference per run.

This vignette stays on the spine: simulate a dataset with known truth, fit it, read the estimates, predict, compare. It then takes one short taste of each model family, fits a random effect, and walks the standard S3 accessors. The dedicated vignettes go deeper on each family, and the taste tests link out to them rather than repeating their depth here.

A first occupancy model

simulate_occu() draws a single-season dataset with parameters you set, so the fit has a truth to recover. Occupancy depends on one site covariate (occ_cov1) with intercept 0.3 and slope 1.0; detection depends on det_cov1 with intercept 0.7 (so detection probability is about 0.67) and slope 0.6. Six visits per site keep the two processes identifiable.

sim <- simulate_occu(
  N = 300, J = 6,
  n.occ.covs = 1, n.det.covs = 1,
  beta.occ = c(0.3, 1.0),    # occupancy intercept + slope on occ_cov1
  beta.det = c(0.7, 0.6),    # detection intercept + slope on det_cov1
  seed = 1
)
dat <- sim$data              # site covariates, one row per site
y   <- sim$y                 # 300 x 6 detection-history matrix
y[1:3, ]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6]
#> [1,]    0    0    0    0    0    0
#> [2,]    0    0    0    0    0    0
#> [3,]    1    0    1    1    1    1

The simulated object carries three pieces. sim$data is the site frame, one row per site, holding the covariates the occupancy and detection formulas will read. sim$y is the detection history, a matrix with one row per site and one column per visit, each entry a 0 or 1. sim$truth holds the parameters and the latent occupancy state, which the fit never sees and which you keep only to check recovery. Real data arrive without that last piece, so the recovery checks here are a luxury of working from a simulation; on a field dataset you fit, predict, and compare without a truth to measure against.

The raw proportion of sites with any detection understates true occupancy, because an occupied site can go undetected on every visit.

c(naive_occupied = mean(rowSums(y) > 0),
  true_occupied  = mean(sim$truth$z))
#> naive_occupied  true_occupied 
#>      0.5800000      0.5833333

The gap between those two numbers is the whole reason an occupancy model exists. The naive rate counts a site as occupied only if the species was seen at least once, and with detection near two thirds across six visits a present species is missed on every visit about one time in a thousand, so the gap is small here. Cut the visits to two or the detection to 0.3 and the gap widens fast, because a present species then slips through undetected often enough to drag the observed rate well below the truth. The model recovers the difference by reading how often a species seen on one visit was missed on the next.

The mechanism is worth one sentence before the fit. Across six visits an occupied site at detection pp produces at least one sighting with probability 1−(1−p)61 - (1 - p)^6, so the fraction of occupied sites that never register a single detection is (1−p)6(1 - p)^6. Invert that and the observed detection rate tells you both how many occupied sites you missed and what pp must have been to miss them, provided you have enough visits for the two to separate. Six visits at detection 0.67 leave almost no occupied site silent, which is why the naive and true rates nearly agree here and why this design recovers cleanly. The same model run on a two-visit survey would carry a wide interval on pp and a noticeably higher estimated occupancy than the naive count, because more occupied sites would have gone unseen.

Fit the proper model with tobs(). The latent occupancy formula is the first argument, detection is its own formula, and occu() selects the single-season family. method = "laplace" is the default: it finds the posterior mode and the curvature there and returns in a fraction of a second.

fit <- tobs(
  ~ occ_cov1,
  data      = dat,
  family    = occu(),
  detection = ~ det_cov1,
  y         = y,
  method    = "laplace",
  control   = list(verbose = FALSE)   # the EM prints its iterations otherwise
)

Five arguments carry the whole model, and they map one to one onto the two-level structure. The first formula is the occupancy linear predictor on the logit of ψ\psi. The detection formula is the per-visit detection predictor on the logit of pp. The family names the likelihood, here single-season occupancy. The y matrix is the observation. The method picks the inference. Everything that is not a statistical choice (verbosity, iteration caps, tolerances, thread counts) lives inside control, so the call signature stays statistical and the knobs stay in one place. Swapping occu() for abun() and handing it a count matrix turns the same call into an N-mixture fit; the shape does not change.

coef() returns the estimates as one vector, each name carrying the process and the coefficient (psi_occ_cov1). The occupancy and detection coefficients both land near the simulated truth.

coef(fit)
#> psi_(Intercept)    psi_occ_cov1   p_(Intercept)      p_det_cov1 
#>       0.3638670       1.0118715       0.6744931       0.5087683

coef(fit, arm = "psi") holds the occupancy intercept and the slope on occ_cov1, both on the logit scale, and coef(fit, arm = "p") holds the detection coefficients. Reading the occupancy intercept of about 0.3 through plogis() gives a baseline occupancy near 0.57 at the covariate mean; the slope of about 1.0 says occupancy rises steeply with occ_cov1. Keep the link in mind whenever you read a coefficient: occupancy and detection are both logit-scale, so a coefficient is a change in log-odds, not in probability, and the mapping to probability is steepest near the middle of the range and flat at the ends.

The per-process list is the shape every family in the package returns, so the same line of code reads the right block whatever the model. A single-season occupancy fit has psi and p; an N-mixture fit has lambda and p; an integrated fit has one occupancy block and a detection block per source. Reaching into the named element rather than a flat coefficient vector keeps the two arms distinct, which matters because they live on different links and mean different things. A common slip is to back-transform the whole vector with one function; the occupancy intercept needs plogis() to read as a probability, while an abundance intercept needs exp() to read as a count, and mixing them produces numbers that look plausible and are wrong.

summary() adds the posterior standard deviation and the 2.5%/50%/97.5% credible bounds for every coefficient. The psi_ rows are the occupancy linear predictor, the p_ rows the detection one.

summary(fit)
#>                  estimate  std.error     2.5 %    97.5 %
#> psi_(Intercept) 0.3638670 0.12974646 0.1095686 0.6181653
#> psi_occ_cov1    1.0118715 0.15488654 0.7082995 1.3154436
#> p_(Intercept)   0.6744931 0.06861693 0.5400064 0.8089798
#> p_det_cov1      0.5087683 0.06957512 0.3724036 0.6451330

Read the summary as four numbers per coefficient: the posterior mean, its standard deviation, and the lower and upper credible bounds. The bounds are the honest report. A slope whose interval clears zero is doing work; one whose interval straddles zero is consistent with no effect regardless of how large the point estimate looks. Here the occupancy slope on occ_cov1 sits well clear of zero, which is the signal the simulation built in. The standard deviation and the bounds come straight from the curvature of the log-posterior at the mode, so the Laplace fit reports them without a sampling step.

confint() returns the same bounds as a matrix, reading the fixed-effect block of the Hessian the Laplace fit already computed, so there is no extra sampling step.

confint(fit)
#>                     2.5 %    97.5 %
#> psi_(Intercept) 0.1095686 0.6181653
#> psi_occ_cov1    0.7082995 1.3154436
#> p_(Intercept)   0.5400064 0.8089798
#> p_det_cov1      0.3724036 0.6451330

Occupancy, detection, and the latent state

fitted() returns three per-site quantities: psi (the modelled occupancy probability), p (detection probability), and z (the posterior probability the site is occupied given its detection history). A site with at least one detection has z = 1; a site with all-zero visits gets the partial credit the model assigns from psi and p.

fv <- fitted(fit)
str(lapply(fv, head, 4))
#> List of 3
#>  $ psi: num [1:4] 0.433 0.634 0.382 0.878
#>  $ p  : num [1:4] 0.756 0.535 0.843 0.618
#>  $ z  : num [1:4] 0.000162 0.017137 1 1

The three quantities answer three different questions about a site. psi is what the model expects before seeing the visits: the occupancy probability the covariates imply. p is the per-visit detection probability the covariates imply. z is the posterior after the visits: given what was actually recorded, how sure are we the site is occupied. A site detected once has z = 1 because detection rules out absence. A site with six blank visits has a z below one, pulled down from psi by the chance that six visits at this detection would all miss a present species. That posterior occupancy is the quantity richness sums over in a community model, and it is the right thing to map when you want occupancy rather than detections.

The three numbers also pull apart the two ways a model can be wrong about a site. If psi is high but the visits are all blank and z stays high, the model is saying the covariates expect occupancy and the few visits were not enough to overturn that expectation. If psi is low and z is also low, the model and the data agree the site is probably empty. The disagreements are the interesting cases: a low psi with a detection pulling z up means the species turned up somewhere the covariates did not predict, which is the kind of residual a map of z minus psi makes visible. Reading the three together, rather than any one alone, is how you tell a confident prediction from a guess the covariates had to make.

Plotting the fitted psi against the true occupancy probability shows the model recovers the site-level signal, not just the population mean.

plot(sim$truth$psi, fv$psi, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.35),
     xlab = "true psi", ylab = "fitted psi")
abline(0, 1, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

The points scatter along the identity line rather than collapsing onto a single horizontal band, which is the test that matters. A model that recovered only the population mean would predict the same psi for every site and the cloud would be flat. This one tracks the covariate-driven spread, so a site with high occ_cov1 is predicted high and a low one low. The scatter around the line is the irreducible uncertainty six binary visits leave behind, not bias.

Laplace and NUTS

The Laplace fit conditions on a Gaussian posterior shape. That is exact for the fixed-effect curvature here and immediate to compute. When you want draws from the full posterior, method = "nuts" runs the gradient sampler; it reports Rhat and effective sample size alongside the estimates.

fit_nuts <- tobs(
  ~ occ_cov1,
  data      = dat,
  family    = occu(),
  detection = ~ det_cov1,
  y         = y,
  method    = "nuts",
  control   = list(n.iter = 800, n.warmup = 400, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
)
summary(fit_nuts)
#>                  estimate  std.error     2.5 %    97.5 %     rhat ess_bulk
#> psi_(Intercept) 0.3726613 0.12659745 0.1356939 0.6362571 1.018267 463.9132
#> psi_occ_cov1    1.0340742 0.16176800 0.7285672 1.3700560 1.008509 629.9656
#> p_(Intercept)   0.6754331 0.06668084 0.5536290 0.8116605 1.012013 424.4801
#> p_det_cov1      0.5146168 0.06223141 0.3899390 0.6464447 1.000245 375.8263
#>                 ess_tail
#> psi_(Intercept) 448.1412
#> psi_occ_cov1    504.2690
#> p_(Intercept)   404.8984
#> p_det_cov1      302.2130

The two backends agree on the coefficients to within their uncertainty. Rhat near 1 and effective sample sizes in the hundreds say the chains mixed. With six visits and detection near 0.67 the Laplace mode and the posterior mean coincide; at fewer visits or lower detection the joint mode can drift, and NUTS is the honest choice.

The two diagnostics report different things, and a fit is trustworthy only when both pass. Rhat compares the variance within each chain to the variance across chains; a value near 1 means the chains explored the same region and agree on it, while a value above about 1.01 says they have not converged on a common answer and the summaries are premature. Effective sample size discounts the autocorrelation in the chain: a thousand draws that wander slowly might carry the information of only a few dozen independent ones, and a small effective sample size means the reported standard error is itself noisy. The Laplace fit reports neither, because it has no chains; its summaries come from the curvature at the mode, which is exact for the fixed-effect block and immediate. The decision between the two is not Laplace-versus-NUTS in general but per run: fast and deterministic when the posterior is well behaved, sampled when it is skewed or weakly identified.

data.frame(
  term    = names(coef(fit)),
  laplace = round(coef(fit), 3),
  nuts    = round(coef(fit_nuts), 3),
  row.names = NULL
)
#>              term laplace  nuts
#> 1 psi_(Intercept)   0.364 0.373
#> 2    psi_occ_cov1   1.012 1.034
#> 3   p_(Intercept)   0.674 0.675
#> 4      p_det_cov1   0.509 0.515

Prediction

tobs_marginal_effect() varies one covariate across its range, holds the others at their mean, and returns the predicted probability with a credible band. Here it traces how occupancy responds to occ_cov1.

me <- tobs_marginal_effect(fit_nuts, "occ_cov1", process = "occupancy")
plot(me)

The curve rises across the covariate range because the occupancy slope is positive, and the band widens at the ends where the data thin out. The process argument switches the same call to the detection arm; pass process = "detection" and the same machinery traces pp against one of its covariates instead. Either way the result is a tidy table you can plot with the built-in method or feed to your own ggplot.

For prediction at an explicit design, pass a matrix to X.0 with one column per occupancy coefficient. The result carries the posterior mean, SD, and credible bounds of psi at each new row.

X0 <- cbind(`(Intercept)` = 1, occ_cov1 = c(-1, 0, 1))
predict(fit_nuts, X.0 = X0)
#>        mean         sd      q2.5       q50     q97.5
#> 1 0.3416830 0.04209410 0.2669885 0.3393469 0.4249586
#> 2 0.5917456 0.03045209 0.5338715 0.5928335 0.6539069
#> 3 0.8009468 0.03456605 0.7300807 0.8013661 0.8633308

The three rows ask for occupancy at occ_cov1 of -1, 0, and 1 with the intercept held in. The returned mean climbs across the rows and each row carries its own credible bounds, which is the prediction you would map across a landscape: build X.0 from the covariate raster, predict, and plot the posterior mean with its band. A ggplot of the marginal effect draws the same picture as a smooth curve, with the band carried straight from the prediction table.

ggplot(me, aes(x = x, y = estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "occ_cov1", y = "occupancy probability") +
  transparent

Random effects

Surveys carry structure that is not a covariate of interest: sites fall into clusters, observers differ in effort, regions sit under their own unmeasured baseline. A grouping factor with many exchangeable levels belongs in a random effect, which assumes the level effects are draws from a common distribution N(0,σ2)N(0, \sigma^2) and estimates the spread rather than one free intercept per level. A level with little data is pulled toward the population mean; a level with plenty keeps its own signal. tulpaObs writes random effects the lme4 way, with a bar inside the formula, and (1 | g) enters whichever linear predictor it sits in.

Simulate occupancy that varies by a site cluster: thirty clusters of twenty-five sites, each with its own intercept drawn from N(0,0.92)N(0, 0.9^2), plus one site covariate.

set.seed(101)
ng <- 30L; per <- 25L; N <- ng * per
g  <- rep(seq_len(ng), each = per)
x  <- rnorm(N)
b_true <- rnorm(ng, 0, 0.9)                       # per-cluster intercepts
z  <- rbinom(N, 1, plogis(0.3 - 0.6 * x + b_true[g]))
y_re <- matrix(0L, N, 6L)
for (i in seq_len(N)) y_re[i, ] <- rbinom(6L, 1, z[i] * 0.45)
d_re <- data.frame(g = factor(g), x = x)

Put (1 | g) in the occupancy formula. The default Laplace path fits the variance component through a variance-component EM with an adaptive Gauss-Hermite debias for small clusters; coef() returns the fixed effects and ranef() the per-group BLUPs.

fit_re <- tobs(~ x + (1 | g), data = d_re, y = y_re, detection = ~ 1,
               family = occu(), method = "laplace",
               control = list(verbose = FALSE))
coef(fit_re, arm = "psi")
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>   0.2369320  -0.6833076

The variance component lands in fit$means, named for the group it belongs to, and the per-cluster intercepts come back from ranef() as a table with one row per group. Plotting the recovered BLUPs against the simulated cluster effects shows the random effect tracks the cluster-level signal, with the shrinkage that pulls thin clusters toward zero.

re <- ranef(fit_re)
bl <- data.frame(truth = b_true, blup = re$estimate)
ggplot(bl, aes(x = truth, y = blup)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "true cluster effect", y = "estimated BLUP") +
  transparent

The estimated intercepts line up along the identity with a slight pull toward zero, the shrinkage the random effect applies where a cluster’s own data are thin. Correlated random slopes (1 + x | g), the uncorrelated form (x || g), crossed (1 | g:h), and nested (1 | g/h) grouping all fit the same way, and a bar in the detection formula moves the random effect onto the detection arm instead. The dedicated treatment, including the small-cluster bias and when to reach for NUTS, is in vignette("random-effects").

Comparing models

waic() computes the widely applicable information criterion from the pointwise log-likelihood. Lower is better. Compare the covariate model against an intercept-only occupancy model to check the covariate earns its place.

fit0 <- tobs(~ 1, data = dat, family = occu(),
             detection = ~ det_cov1, y = y, method = "laplace",
             control = list(verbose = FALSE))

c(intercept_only = waic(fit0)$estimates["waic", "Estimate"],
  with_covariate = waic(fit)$estimates["waic", "Estimate"])
#> intercept_only with_covariate 
#>       1695.451       1646.075

The covariate model has the lower WAIC, matching how the data were generated. The drop reflects the occupancy slope the intercept-only model cannot represent.

The same comparison weighs the random effect. Fit the clustered data with and without the grouping term, then read the two WAICs side by side. The random-intercept model should win when the clusters genuinely differ, because the flat model has nowhere to put the between-cluster variance and predicts the clustered sites worse.

fit_re0 <- tobs(~ x, data = d_re, y = y_re, detection = ~ 1,
                family = occu(), method = "laplace",
                control = list(verbose = FALSE))

c(no_random_effect = waic(fit_re0)$estimates["waic", "Estimate"],
  with_random_int  = waic(fit_re)$estimates["waic", "Estimate"])
#> no_random_effect  with_random_int 
#>         4347.346         4354.090

The clustered model carries the lower WAIC, the random intercept paying for its one variance parameter by predicting the between-cluster spread the flat model averages away. waic() returns a loo waic object whose $estimates table carries more than the headline number: waic is the criterion, elpd_waic the expected log pointwise predictive density it is built from, and p_waic the effective number of parameters, which is what docks a flexible model for its complexity. Two fits compare directly with loo::loo_compare(waic(fit0), waic(fit)). Read WAIC as a comparison, not a verdict: a lower value says one model predicts the in-sample data better, not that its intervals are calibrated. Pair it with a posterior-predictive check (ppc()) before trusting a fit. The full model-comparison and diagnostic workflow is in vignette("diagnostics").

Taste tests

The same call shape fits counts, communities, cover, and the spatial, dynamic, and integrated extensions; only family, the response, and a formula term or two change. These are tastes, one short fit each, with a plot and a pointer to the vignette that goes deep.

Single-season occupancy

The model from the worked example is the base case, and it is worth seeing its output as a print rather than a coefficient list. The print method lays out both processes with their estimates and the family that produced them, which is the first thing you read off a fresh fit.

fit
#> <tobs_fit: single-season occupancy>
#>   family         : occu (status: working)
#>   default method : laplace
#> 
#>   Sites: 300, Max visits: 6
#>   Samples: 1000
#> 
#> Mean occupancy (intercept): 0.590
#> Mean detection (intercept): 0.663

A bar plot of the two occupancy coefficients against zero reads the model at a glance: the slope clears zero, the intercept sits where the baseline occupancy puts it. The same picture for the detection arm comes from coef(fit, arm = "p").

co <- data.frame(term = names(coef(fit, arm = "psi")), est = coef(fit, arm = "psi"))
ggplot(co, aes(x = term, y = est)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "estimate (logit scale)") +
  transparent

Single-season occupancy is the spine the other families extend, and the identifiability tension between occupancy and detection runs through all of them. The tension has a simple source: a string of zeros at a site is consistent with absence and with a present species missed on every visit, and only the repeat visits and the covariates pull the two apart. When the visits are few or detection is low, the likelihood flattens along the ridge where occupancy and detection trade off, the mode becomes a poor summary, and the Laplace standard errors run optimistic. The same fit under NUTS traces the ridge and reports the honest, wider interval. Where recovery fails, how visits and detection trade off, and how to read a model that has too few visits to separate the two are worked through in vignette("occupancy").

N-mixture abundance

abun() fits Royle’s N-mixture model: a latent count per site drawn from a Poisson, thinned by binomial detection on each visit. The abundance arm uses a log link, so its intercept back-transforms with exp(). The fit reads the spread of counts across visits to separate abundance from detection.

sa <- simulate_abun(N = 200, J = 5, n.abund.covs = 1, n.det.covs = 1,
                    beta.lambda = c(log(3), 0.5), beta.p = c(0.4, 0.3),
                    seed = 2)
fa <- tobs(~ abund_cov1, data = sa$data, family = abun(),
           detection = ~ det_cov1, y = sa$y, method = "laplace",
           control = list(verbose = FALSE))
exp(coef(fa, arm = "lambda")[["(Intercept)"]])    # baseline expected abundance
#> [1] 2.907134

The back-transformed intercept lands near the simulated baseline of three animals per site. Predicting abundance across the covariate range and plotting it shows the log-linear rise on the response scale.

pr <- predict(fa, terms = "abund_cov1")
ggplot(pr, aes(x = x, y = estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "abund_cov1", y = "expected abundance") +
  transparent

The curve climbs because the abundance slope is positive, and the band carries the count uncertainty through the exponential. What lets the model see eight animals through counts that never reach eight is the spread of the counts across visits. A site that averages two animals per visit could hold twenty seen one time in ten or three seen two times in three, and the two readings produce counts with very different variance: many animals at low detection jump around relative to their mean, few at high detection barely move. The N-mixture reads that spread and infers the abundance behind it, which is why replicate visits are not optional here. The model also leans on closure, that the same animals stay put across the survey window, so a season long enough to let animals move violates it and reads the movement as detection noise. abun(mixture = "negbin") adds an overdispersion parameter for counts with more spread than a Poisson allows, common when animals cluster, and the same icar() / bym2() terms that smooth occupancy smooth a count surface. The closure assumption, the count ceiling KK, the negative-binomial state, and areal spatial counts are in vignette("abundance").

Community models

ms_occu() fits many species at once, with community-level hyperpriors tying the species coefficients together so a rare species borrows the shape of the assemblage. y is a sites-by-visits-by-species array and species names the third dimension. The community mean is the fixed effect coef() returns.

sm <- simulate_ms_occu(N = 120, J = 5, n.species = 8, seed = 3)
fm <- tobs(~ x, data = sm$data, family = ms_occu(), detection = ~ 1,
           y = sm$y, species = paste0("sp", 1:8), method = "laplace",
           control = list(verbose = FALSE))
coef(fm, arm = "psi")                                # community occupancy mean
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>  -0.1803196   0.5286092

tobs_richness() turns the per-species occupancy posteriors into a site-level species-richness estimate with uncertainty, summing occupancy probabilities across species rather than counting detections. Plotting richness against site, ordered, shows the spread across the survey with its band.

rich <- tobs_richness(fm)
rich <- rich[order(rich$mean), ]
rich$site <- seq_len(nrow(rich))
ggplot(rich, aes(x = site, y = mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5), alpha = 0.25, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "site (ordered by richness)", y = "expected richness") +
  transparent

The modelled richness exceeds the naive detected count because it adds the species probably present but undetected, and the band carries every species’ occupancy uncertainty into the sum. The reason to fit the assemblage jointly rather than species by species is the rare species. A bird seen at three sites out of a hundred carries almost no information on its own, and its single-species slope would run from deeply negative to deeply positive. The community prior assumes the species coefficients are draws from a shared distribution and pulls a thin species toward the assemblage mean, hardest where its own data are weakest. The pull strength is the fitted community covariance, learned from how the species scatter rather than set by hand, so a homogeneous assemblage pools hard and a heterogeneous one barely pools at all. The count analogue is ms_abun(), the community N-mixture, which pools abundance and detection across the assemblage the same way and exposes per-species deviations through ranef(). When pooling helps, when it hurts, and how to read the community covariance are in vignette("community-models").

Cover hurdle

cover() fits a hurdle for continuous vegetation cover: a binomial occurrence process on whether the species is present at all, plus a positive-cover process (lognormal or beta) for how much ground it covers where it occurs. The two arms fit as independent Laplace approximations, and predict() reads occupancy and expected cover at new covariate values.

sc <- simulate_cover(N = 400, beta.occ = c(-0.4, 0.7),
                     beta.pos = c(-1.0, 0.3), sigma.pos = 0.4, seed = 7)
fc <- tobs(~ x, data = sc$data, family = cover(response = "lognormal"),
           y = sc$y)
nd <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 50))
nd$expected <- predict(fc, nd, type = "expected")
head(nd)
#>           x   expected
#> 1 -2.000000 0.03160168
#> 2 -1.918367 0.03393849
#> 3 -1.836735 0.03643353
#> 4 -1.755102 0.03909579
#> 5 -1.673469 0.04193459
#> 6 -1.591837 0.04495957

The expected-cover curve combines both arms: the chance the species occurs times the cover it carries where it does. Plotting it across the covariate range traces the unconditional expected cover.

nd$occupancy <- predict(fc, nd, type = "occupancy")
ggplot(nd, aes(x = x, y = expected)) +
  geom_line(colour = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "expected cover") +
  transparent

The rise reflects both a higher occurrence probability and more cover where present as the covariate climbs. Cover data have a shape that breaks an ordinary regression: a pile of exact zeros where the species is absent, and a continuous positive distribution where it occurs. Modelling the two together with one Gaussian forces a single mean to explain both the zeros and the spread, and it predicts impossible negative cover at the low end. The hurdle splits them, a binomial arm on presence and a positive arm on the cover where present, so the zeros inform occurrence and the positive values inform the cover distribution without contaminating each other. The expected cover the plot shows is the product of the two arms, which is why it can rise both because the species occurs more often and because it covers more ground where it does. This dispatcher predicts from fixed effects only; the shared-field joint model, where occurrence, detection, and cover couple through one spatial field, is the occu_cover() family. The independent-arm hurdle is in vignette("cover-hurdle"), and the joint engine in vignette("cover-hurdle-motivate").

Spatial occupancy

A neighbourhood graph lets adjacent regions share what the covariates miss. An areal spatial field adds one smoothed random effect per cell, ties neighbours together, and soaks up the part of occupancy that depends on where a cell sits. The fields are formula terms: icar(), bym2(), and car_proper(), each taking a dense 0/1 adjacency matrix. They route through method = "nested_laplace", which integrates the smoothing strength over a grid.

gx <- 5; n <- gx * gx
coord <- expand.grid(cx = seq_len(gx), cy = seq_len(gx))
adj <- matrix(0, n, n)
for (i in seq_len(gx)) for (j in seq_len(gx)) {
  a <- (j - 1) * gx + i
  if (i < gx) { b <- (j - 1) * gx + i + 1; adj[a, b] <- adj[b, a] <- 1 }
  if (j < gx) { b <- j * gx + i;           adj[a, b] <- adj[b, a] <- 1 }
}
field <- 1.4 * exp(-((coord$cx - 3)^2 + (coord$cy - 3)^2) / 4)
field <- field - mean(field)
z <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(field))
ys <- matrix(0L, n, 8L)
for (i in seq_len(n)) if (z[i]) ys[i, ] <- rbinom(8L, 1, 0.5)
fit_sp <- tobs(~ bym2(graph = adj), data = data.frame(site = seq_len(n)),
               family = occu(), detection = ~ 1, y = ys,
               method = "nested_laplace",
               control = list(max.iter = 30L, tol = 1e-5, verbose = FALSE))

predict(type = "state") returns the smoothed per-cell occupancy posterior. Laying it back on the grid coordinates and shading each cell maps the field, which peaks where the simulated bump put it.

sp <- predict(fit_sp, type = "state")
mp <- cbind(coord, psi = sp$psi)
ggplot(mp, aes(x = cx, y = cy, fill = psi)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "psi") +
  transparent

The high-occupancy ridge runs through the grid centre, smoothed from the binary noise an isolated per-cell estimate would carry. The field earns its keep two ways. It widens the slope standard errors to their honest size, because adjacent cells share unmeasured drivers and a non-spatial fit treats them as independent and runs its errors too narrow. And it keeps a patterned covariate from absorbing the regional signal it competes with, so the fitted slope reads against a background that already accounts for location. The smoothing strength is itself a parameter, and the nested path integrates it over a grid rather than fixing it, so the slope errors inherit the field’s uncertainty instead of pretending the smoothing was known. ICAR is the plain smoother, BYM2 splits structured from unstructured variation, and the proper CAR estimates the autocorrelation strength. Areal fields, the floating intercept under ICAR, and held-out-cell interpolation are in vignette("spatial-occupancy"); continuous fields on point coordinates are in vignette("occupancy-spatial-spde").

Dynamic occupancy

dyn_occu() fits the multi-season model of MacKenzie and colleagues: a first-season occupancy, a colonisation rate for empty sites, an extinction rate for occupied sites, and a detection process over the latent state. The response carries a season dimension, and the model sums the latent Markov chain out with the forward algorithm.

sd_dyn <- simulate_dyn_occu(N = 200, J = 4, n.seasons = 6,
                            beta.occ = c(0), beta.det = c(0),
                            gamma = 0.3, epsilon = 0.2, seed = 2026)
fit_dyn <- tobs(~ 1, data = sd_dyn$data, family = dyn_occu(),
                detection = ~ 1, y = sd_dyn$y,
                colonization = ~ 1, extinction = ~ 1,
                method = "laplace", control = list(verbose = FALSE))
fit_dyn$intercepts                          # psi1, p, gamma, epsilon
#> $psi1
#> psi1_(Intercept) 
#>        0.4709663 
#> 
#> $p
#> p_(Intercept) 
#>     0.5012209 
#> 
#> $gamma
#> gamma_(Intercept) 
#>         0.2985127 
#> 
#> $epsilon
#> epsilon_(Intercept) 
#>           0.2100606

The four rates land near their simulated values. The two transition rates imply an equilibrium occupancy γ/(γ+ϵ)\gamma / (\gamma + \epsilon), and iterating the transition forward from ψ1\psi_1 draws the modelled trajectory across seasons against the realised occupancy fractions.

g <- fit_dyn$intercepts$gamma; e <- fit_dyn$intercepts$epsilon
ns <- dim(sd_dyn$y)[3]; psi_t <- numeric(ns); psi_t[1] <- fit_dyn$intercepts$psi1
for (t in 2:ns) psi_t[t] <- psi_t[t - 1] * (1 - e) + (1 - psi_t[t - 1]) * g
tj <- data.frame(season = seq_len(ns), realised = colMeans(sd_dyn$truth$z),
                 modelled = psi_t)
ggplot(tj, aes(x = season)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = modelled), colour = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = realised)) +
  ylim(0, 1) + labs(y = "occupied fraction") + transparent

The modelled curve rises from the fitted starting occupancy toward the equilibrium the rates imply, tracking the realised fractions. The reason to estimate the two rates rather than occupancy alone is that the same standing occupancy can come from opposite dynamics. A level holding at sixty percent could be a placid system where the same sites stay occupied for years, or a churning one where many sites wink out each season and as many are colonised. The static occupancy is identical; the rates tell them apart, and they imply different conservation responses. The model reads the rates from the pattern of which sites change state between consecutive seasons, which is why a multi-season survey is worth the extra effort over repeating a single-season one. Covariates on colonisation and extinction, turnover, and the count analogue dyn_abun() are in vignette("dynamic-occupancy").

Integrated occupancy

int_occu() combines several data sources that disagree about detection but agree about occupancy. The sources share one latent occupancy state and each carries its own detection process, so a structured survey anchors the calibration while opportunistic records extend the reach. y is a list of detection-history matrices, one per source.

si <- simulate_int_occu(N.total = 500, n.data = 2, J = c(2, 5),
                        n.shared = 250, beta.occ = c(0.3, 0.9),
                        beta.det = list(c(0.5, 0), c(0.7, 0)), seed = 11)
fit_int <- tobs(~ x, data = si$data, family = int_occu(), detection = ~ 1,
                y = list(survey = si$y[[1]], casual = si$y[[2]]),
                method = "laplace", control = list(verbose = FALSE))
coef(fit_int, arm = "psi")                           # shared occupancy block
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>   0.1627076   0.7712881

The fit returns one shared occupancy block plus a detection block per source, keyed by the names you gave y. Plotting the two detection intercepts on the probability scale shows each source’s reporting rate, estimated separately.

dp <- data.frame(source = c("survey", "casual"),
                 p = plogis(c(coef(fit_int, arm = "survey"), coef(fit_int, arm = "casual"))))
ggplot(dp, aes(x = source, y = p)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.5) +
  ylim(0, 1) + labs(x = NULL, y = "detection probability") +
  transparent

The two bars sit at different heights because the sources detect at different rates, which is the point of the separate detection blocks. The shared state borrows strength from both; the detection arms stay independent. The logic that makes integration pay is that occupancy is a property of the place and the species, not of who is looking, so a structured survey and a casual stream can share one zz while keeping their own pp. A single thin source has to estimate occupancy and its own detection from a few visits, and the two trade off; a second source that observes overlapping sites brings more visits to bear on the shared state without forcing the detection processes to match. The gain scales with the overlap and with how much real occupancy signal the added source carries. Where integration sharpens the occupancy slope, the overlap that drives the gain, and source-specific detection covariates are in vignette("integrated-occupancy"). The joint species distribution family jsdm() and the detection-protocol families removal(), distance(), and fp_occu() extend the same observation layer.

S3 methods

The fitted object answers the standard R accessors, and they behave the same on a Laplace fit and a NUTS fit; the Laplace tier reports the Gaussian approximation at the mode, the sampler tier reports empirical posterior summaries. print() lays out both processes and the family. summary() adds the standard deviation and credible bounds, plus Rhat and effective sample size under NUTS. coef() returns the estimates as a named vector, confint() the credible intervals as a matrix, and vcov() the fixed-effect covariance.

co  <- coef(fit)            # named <process>_<coefficient>
ci  <- confint(fit)         # matrix of credible bounds
vc  <- vcov(fit)            # fixed-effect covariance
list(coef = names(co), confint_rows = rownames(ci), vcov_dim = dim(vc))
#> $coef
#> [1] "psi_(Intercept)" "psi_occ_cov1"    "p_(Intercept)"   "p_det_cov1"     
#> 
#> $confint_rows
#> [1] "psi_(Intercept)" "psi_occ_cov1"    "p_(Intercept)"   "p_det_cov1"     
#> 
#> $vcov_dim
#> [1] 4 4

Beyond the four above, fitted() returns the per-site psi, p, and z; ranef() returns the group-level random effects when a model carries them; residuals() returns deviance, Pearson, or response residuals; predict() returns occupancy at a new design or a varied term; and simulate() draws replicate detection histories from the fit. The plot() method on a prediction object draws the marginal-effect curve with its band, and on a data object summarises the detection histories. The accessor surface is deliberately the base-R one, so a tobs_fit drops into code written for lm or glmer outputs.

The accessors that involve uncertainty read it from whichever inference produced the fit, without you having to ask. On a Laplace fit, confint() and vcov() come from the curvature of the log-posterior at the mode, so they are the Gaussian approximation and they return instantly. On a NUTS fit, the same calls summarise the posterior draws, so the interval is the empirical quantile of the chain and summary() carries the Rhat and effective-sample-size columns alongside. The code you write does not change between the two; only the numbers and their provenance do. That is the practical payoff of keeping the observation layer thin and the inference in the engine: you choose the backend per run and read the result through one set of methods.

Accessor Returns
coef() per-process fixed-effect estimates
summary() estimate, SD, credible bounds (plus Rhat/ESS under NUTS)
confint() credible intervals (matrix)
vcov() fixed-effect covariance
ranef() group-level random effects (when present)
fitted() per-site psi, p, z
predict() occupancy at a new design or varied term
waic() WAIC, elpd, effective parameters
residuals() deviance / Pearson / response residuals
simulate() replicate detection histories from the fit

Practical guidance

  • Start with method = "laplace". It is deterministic and returns in well under a second on a few hundred sites. Use it for the first look and for WAIC comparison. Move to method = "nuts" when detection is low, visits are few, or you need the full posterior shape rather than a Gaussian approximation at the mode.
  • Visits drive identifiability. Occupancy and detection trade off against each other. With two or three visits and detection below about 0.3, the two processes are weakly separated and the Laplace mode can drift; NUTS or more visits resolve it. The identifiability discussion in vignette("occupancy") works through where recovery fails.
  • Detection covariates broadcast across visits when the data frame has one row per site, as in simulate_occu(). For covariates that change between visits (effort, observer, weather), pass a per-visit design; see vignette("data-formatting").
  • Read uncertainty, not just point estimates. confint() and the summary() quantile columns carry the credible bounds. A coefficient whose interval spans zero is not pulling its weight regardless of the point estimate.
  • WAIC compares, it does not validate. A lower WAIC says one model predicts the in-sample data better; it does not say the model is calibrated. Pair it with a posterior-predictive check (ppc(), see vignette("diagnostics")).
